bib.title: Support Vector Machines (Chapter 9, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python)
bib.venue: Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer Nature Switzerland AG

question: How do maximal margin classifiers, support vector classifiers and SVMs work, how do they extend to non-linear boundaries and more than two classes, and how do they relate to logistic regression?
contributions: Introduces maximal margin classifier, support vector classifier, SVM with kernels, multiclass extensions, and the hinge-loss link to logistic regression, with a Python lab (sklearn) and exercises.

results.claim: Hyperplane classifier's margin M is maximised subject to sum beta_j^2 = 1; slack budget C bounds sum eps_i; at most C observations can be on the wrong side of the hyperplane; C=0 recovers the maximal margin classifier.
results.quote: For C > 0 no more than C observa-

results.claim: Large C gives a wide margin, many support vectors, low variance and high bias; small C gives narrow margin, few support vectors, low bias and high variance. Fig 9.7 bottom right has eight support vectors.
results.setup: Fig 9.7, four values of C, simulated 2D data
results.quote: with only eight support vectors
results.note: Note the lab (sklearn) reverses the convention: sklearn C is a cost, so small C gives wide margins (p.387). The text says so itself.

results.claim: Support vector classifier equals hinge loss plus ridge penalty; small lambda corresponds to small C in the budget formulation.
results.quote: a small value of λ in (9.25) amounts to a small value of C
results.note: Consistent with the budget form: large lambda tolerates more violations, like large C; small lambda like small C.

results.claim: Hinge loss is exactly zero when y_i f(x_i) >= 1; logistic loss is nowhere exactly zero but very small far from the boundary; hence SVM and logistic regression often give very similar results.
results.quote: logistic regression and the support vector classifier often give very similar results

results.claim: Rule of thumb: when classes are well separated SVMs tend to behave better than logistic regression; with more overlap logistic regression is often preferred.
results.quote: When the classes are well separated, SVMs tend to behave better than logistic regression

results.claim: One-versus-one builds K choose 2 classifiers and takes a majority vote; one-versus-all fits K classifiers and picks the class with the largest score beta_0k+...+beta_pk x*.

limits: Authors say optimization and kernel details are beyond the book's scope.
Lab data are tiny simulations (20-100 test points); differences of a few points are not significant.
Heart comparison with LDA is eyeballed from ROC curves, and the text itself says differences are not significant.
The lab text and printed output disagree on tuned parameters (see result notes).
Test-performance claim for small vs large C is asserted, left to Exercise 6.
Pages are book numbering 367-398 in the PDF; PDF page = book page minus 366.
practices: Tune C (or lambda) by cross-validation; do not leave it at a default such as 1 (p.376, p.385).
With p much greater than n (Khan, 2308 genes vs 63 samples) use a linear kernel, extra flexibility is unnecessary (p.394).
Judge SVMs by test, not training, ROC; the most flexible radial gamma wins on training and loses on test (p.383).
Use grid search over both C and gamma for a radial kernel with GridSearchCV (p.391).
Multiclass: sklearn SVC uses one-versus-one or one-versus-rest via decision_function_shape (p.393).
Prefer SVM for well separated classes, logistic regression for overlapping ones (p.385).
Nonlinear kernels are not unique to SVMs; logistic regression can use them too (p.386).
